briefs.label: Morning Brief
briefs.title: Relief on the Horizon: Michigan's Tax Fight Gains Bipartisan Allies as National Rescheduling and Psychedelics Momentum Build
briefs.top: Michigan operators are starting to see real daylight on the 24% wholesale tax — both major-party frontrunners for governor now back repeal, and a Muskegon dispensary/restaurant hybrid shows growth is still happening despite the squeeze. Nationally, DEA's rescheduling machinery is grinding forward into implementation while Compass Pathways just landed an accelerated FDA review for its psilocybin depression drug and Curaleaf makes a bold consolidation play for Aurora Cannabis.

local.text: Fields Cannary in Muskegon is pushing a hospitality-forward format further than most Michigan operators have gone, targeting a fall opening for its dispensary with a full-service restaurant to follow — a bet that experience-driven retail can outrun the tax squeeze.

Not every U.P. operator is retreating: Rize, which runs three Upper Michigan stores, has kept growing by striking cost-sharing deals with suppliers that split the wholesale tax burden instead of eating it alone — and despite the new tax, retail flower prices have only ticked up from roughly $10 to $12, meaning most retailers still aren't passing the full hit to customers.

Political momentum for tax relief is now bipartisan: GOP gubernatorial nominee John James is campaigning on repealing or rolling back the 24% wholesale tax as part of his "Freedom Agenda," while Democratic primary candidate Chris Swanson has separately vowed to work to repeal it — on top of House Bill 6224 and Senate Bill 810 already pending in Lansing.

A local win for operator pushback on surveillance overreach: Jars Cannabis reached a deal with Madison Heights to take down a Flock camera aimed at its parking lot, with the unit coming down pending City Council approval after the chain mounted a sign blocking its view.

The demand story underneath the tax pain is still strong — Michigan retailers sold more product in 2025 than in any year since adult-use launched — even as the state's active retail license count dipped slightly from 845 to 836 year-over-year, a gap for operators to fill rather than a market in retreat.

national.text: DEA rescheduling is moving from theory to paperwork: the agency is now sending a 26-question checklist to Colorado medical cannabis businesses applying for federal protections tied to the Schedule III shift — a sign the process is advancing into real implementation for operators who get ahead of it.

The House is expected to take up Senate-passed legislation this week to delay the looming federal recriminalization of hemp THC products, buying lawmakers more time to craft regulation instead of an outright ban — a reprieve for the broader hemp and adjacent cannabinoid supply chain.

Compass Pathways just got a major regulatory tailwind: the FDA granted the company's rolling NDA submission and review request and awarded COMP360 synthetic psilocybin a Commissioner's National Priority Voucher for treatment-resistant depression, which could shrink the final review window to just one to two months.

Consolidation is heating up at the top of the industry: Curaleaf launched a hostile $4-per-share takeover bid for Canadian rival Aurora Cannabis on August 10, prompting Aurora's board to urge shareholders to take no action while it runs a special committee review.

Distribution infrastructure keeps consolidating around scale players: Nabis, the top licensed cannabis wholesale platform, acquired select assets of California's Humble Cannabis Solutions, adding roughly $13 million in assets and expanding its footprint across NorCal, the Central Coast, and SoCal as the market gears up for a post-rescheduling landscape.
